speaker: Luke Alvezio
main_topic: Assembling long-running, autonomous multi-agent teams for complex software engineering tasks.

key_claims.claim: Intelligence is no longer the bottleneck in software engineering; human attention is.
key_claims.details: Engineers have a backlog of features but can only drive a few forward daily because every task requires human supervision for implementation and review, even though current AI models are smart enough to build them.

key_claims.claim: Tests written after implementation don't catch bugs, they confirm decisions.
key_claims.details: When an agent builds a feature and then writes the tests for it, the tests are shaped by the code, not the original intent. True validation must be independent and adversarial.

key_claims.claim: Serial execution beats parallel execution for multi-agent software development.
key_claims.details: Running multiple agents in parallel on a codebase leads to conflicts, duplicated work, and high coordination overhead that burns tokens without speed gains. Serial execution with structured handoffs allows for clean context and compounding correctness.

key_claims.claim: A model-agnostic architecture provides a compounding advantage.
key_claims.details: No single model is best at planning, implementation, and validation. Locking into one provider constrains you to their weakest capability. Mixing models ensures strict instruction following and avoids training-data bias during validation.

frameworks.name: Five Multi-Agent Strategies
components: Delegation: One agent spawns another for a subtask; the simplest pattern.
Creator-Verifier: One agent builds, a different agent checks; enforces separation of concerns and removes sunk-cost bias.
Direct Communication: Peer-to-peer interaction without a central coordinator; hard to maintain state fragments.
Negotiation: Agents coordinate over shared resources; best when there is a possible win-win outcome.
Broadcast: One agent sends status updates and shared context to many; critical for long-running coherence.

frameworks.name: Missions Three-Role Architecture
components: Orchestrator: Handles planning, defining features, setting milestones, and writing the validation contract before any code is written.
Workers (Child): Handle implementation; they start with fresh context, no accumulated baggage, implement a specific feature, and commit via git.
Validators (Child): Handle adversarial verification; they have never seen the implementation code before running tests or QA.

frameworks.name: Validation Loop
components: Validation Contract: Written by the orchestrator during planning; consists of hundreds of assertions defining correctness independently of implementation.
Scrutiny Validator: Runs traditional checks like test suites, typechecking, linting, and spawns dedicated code review agents.
User-Testing Validator: Acts as a QA engineer; launches the live application, navigates via computer-use, clicks buttons, fills forms, and verifies end-to-end functional flows.

frameworks.name: Structured Handoffs
components: Commands run and their exit codes
Whether procedures defined by the orchestrator were followed

examples.lessons: Demonstrated a 16.5-hour autonomous run where 60% of time and tokens were spent on implementation. Validation never succeeded on the first attempt, proving the system's ability to self-correct by spawning follow-up features. Resulted in a highly robust codebase where 50% of the lines of code were tests, achieving 90% test coverage.

Missions are used to prototype new ideas and features overnight, rapidly build internal tools, execute large-scale refactors and migrations for ML research, and modernize codebases to increase overall agent readiness and productivity.

Factory's proprietary system that combines delegation, creator-verifier, broadcast, and negotiation into a single workflow capable of running autonomously for days.
A set of hundreds of assertions defining what 'done' means for a project, generated before any coding begins to prevent system drift.
The emerging engineering skill of mentally modeling how different LLMs interact, where they fail, and how those failures compound over long-running, multi-day executions.

takeaways: To build agent teams that solve truly difficult problems, developers must transition from single-session chats to asynchronous systems that can run autonomously for days.
Adversarial validation—where the testing agent has no prior knowledge of the implementation code and ideally uses a different underlying model—is necessary to prevent systemic drift.
Serial execution, combined with rigorous, structured written handoffs between agents, is more effective for complex software development than attempting to run multiple agents in parallel.

Utilizing different, specialized models for specific roles (e.g., planning vs. implementation vs. validation) yields better results and avoids the weaknesses inherent in relying on a single model family.
